anatomy.intro: Irregular folds and ridges reshape the blue-green stem into a sculptural mass.

parts.function: The folded surface is part of the succulent cactus stem.
parts.label: Wavy stem fold

parts.function: A small cushion produces the short dark spines.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: The glaucous exterior gives the underlying green stem its blue cast.
parts.label: Blue-grey surface

parts.function: Where growth broadens into a line, it can form a fan instead of a single rounded tip.
parts.label: Growth crest

flowers.text: The normal species bears small greenish-white flowers followed by sweet blue-purple garambullo fruits. Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh describes the berries as 8–20 mm across, about blueberry size, and records their sale in Mexican markets.

growth.note: Monstrose growth makes irregular knobs and branching points; crested growth spreads a growing tip into a line, producing broad fans.

stages.text: The cultivated body begins with irregular lobes and ridges.
stages.title: Small folded plant

stages.text: Different growing regions add uneven new folds or fan-shaped tissue.
stages.title: Changing outline

stages.text: Continued growth builds an individual outline rather than a predictable straight column.
stages.title: Older sculpture

habitat.text: The wild species grows on stony and sandy soils in Mexico’s seasonally dry tropical woodland. Indigo Wave is a cultivated selection with irregular, folded growth.

lookalikes.name: Ming Thing
lookalikes.text: Ming Thing makes thick rounded clubs, while Indigo Wave has blue-green folded ridges and broader fan-like areas.

mature.text: Ordinary Myrtillocactus geometrizans forms a candelabra-like tree around 3.4–4.6 m tall. Indigo Wave retains a folded, irregular outline as its stems expand.

milestones.text: Joined the collection from Altman Reserve.
milestones.title: Acquired

nameStory.text: The species appeared as Cereus geometrizans in 1837 and moved to Myrtillocactus in 1897. The nursery selection is sold as Indigo Wave.
